questions.q: Per this lesson, what is access governance, as distinct from the individual controls in this chapter?
options: The program that decides when each control fires, who's accountable, and how grants are proven correct later
A single software product that replaces all other access controls
A one-time project completed when a company is founded
A synonym for role-based access control
questions.explain: Access governance is the coordinating layer: it schedules and documents controls like RBAC, least privilege, SoD, reviews, and privileged-access management rather than being a separate control itself.

questions.q: In the Joiner-Mover-Leaver lifecycle, which event most often leaves stale access behind if governance doesn't catch it?
options: Mover — new access gets granted, but old access tied to the previous role is nobody's trigger to remove
Joiner — because new hires never get any access
Leaver — because terminated employees always keep full access
None of the three; JML events never cause stale access
questions.explain: A Mover's new manager asks for new access, which gets granted. Removing the old role's access has no natural trigger, which is why access reviews exist as a backstop.

questions.q: Which four roles does this lesson identify in every access decision?
options: Requester, approver, provisioner, auditor
Developer, tester, manager, vendor
Owner, user, guest, administrator
CEO, CFO, CISO, CIO
questions.explain: The requester identifies the need, the approver (typically the data owner) decides if it's justified, the provisioner executes the grant, and the auditor independently confirms it later.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the same person filling both the requester and approver role for their own access request is a problem?
options: It undermines segregation of duties — one person shouldn't be able to request and approve their own access with no one else involved
It is illegal in every jurisdiction
It makes the access request process too slow
It has no real downside as long as the person is trusted
questions.explain: Splitting the requester and approver responsibilities across different people is a form of segregation of duties, covered in depth in Lesson 15.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what happens to an organization that has every individual access control in place but no coordinating access governance program?
options: It can still fail an audit, because nobody can produce evidence of when and why each grant happened
It automatically passes every audit regardless of documentation
It no longer needs least privilege or segregation of duties
It becomes immune to insider threats
questions.explain: Without the coordinating layer that access governance provides, an organization can have strong individual controls and still be unable to demonstrate, with evidence, that access decisions were correct and timely.
